blocks.text: On the Raven that Noah Sent Out of the Ark.

Concerning the raven, the sacred text contains two narratives: one about the raven sent out of the ark by Noah; the other about the ravens that fed Elias in the desert. According to the Hebrews, the former reads as follows, Gen. VIII, 7: And he sent out the raven, and it went out, going forth and returning, until the waters had dried up from the face of the earth. In some copies the Greek edition states the reason for sending out the raven thus: Καὶ ἀπέστειλε τὸν κόρακα ἰδεῖν, εἰ κεκόπακε τὸ ὕδωρ [Kai apesteile ton koraka idein, ei kekopake to hydōr]; And he sent out the raven, to see whether the waters had ceased. This is taken from the following verse, which concerns the dove: He also sent out the dove from him, to see whether the waters had abated from the face of the earth. And indeed it is evident that Noah sent out the raven with the same intention as the dove. But Moses, to avoid the tedium of repetition, stated this only of the dove, whose story he therefore set out more explicitly, because it is of greater importance. So on the first day of the tenth month, when the waters of the flood had decreased considerably, the topmost peaks of the highest mountains had already begun to appear, Gen. VIII, 5. And after forty days had passed, that is, on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Noah opened the window of the ark and sent out the raven. Since forty days of rain had overwhelmed the earth with waters, Gen. VII, 12., Noah had hoped that the waters would dry up in the same number of days. When this did not happen, he sent out the raven, which he knew could be lured by the smell of carcasses to fly farther off, if the earth were already open to animals. But the raven, flying round the ark, did not go far from it. It went out (says Moses) going forth and returning. For once sent out, seeing nothing but foul swamps, it at once sought refuge either in the ark or on top of the ark. Flying off from it again and again, it kept returning; and it did nothing [II, 801] else until the waters had dried up. The Hebrews talk nonsense in the Agudda, saying that the raven did not stop circling the ark, nor go where it had been sent, שהיה חושדו על בת זוגו, because he was anxious about his mate (or female); that is, lest in his absence she be covered by another. Since this cannot be understood of another raven, as Noah had kept only two, I will not add the monstrosities that these impure men, the most senseless of mortals, invent for themselves. In Bereshit Rabbah, section 33, Noah and the raven converse with each other. When the raven asks why, out of all the cattle, [col. 210] wild beasts and birds, he alone was sent, Noah replies that the world could easily do without ravens, since they are useful neither לאכילה, for eating, nor לקרבן, for sacrifices. But God intervenes, warning that in future ages ravens would be of great use, namely in the time of Elias, who was fed for some time on bread and meat brought by ravens. And for that very reason, of course, God did not want the raven to go far from the ark. And He said to it, אתה מזומן לשליחות אחרת בימי אליהו, In the days of Elias you must undertake another mission (of greater importance); and therefore you must be preserved for those times. This, they say, the very words of Moses obscurely hint at when he says עד יבשת, until they had dried up, because the word יבשת has the same letters as the word תשבי Tishbi. Thus עד יבשת means עד תשבי, Until the Tishbite, supply Elias, as Baal Hatturim observes; and he adds that the letters of יבשת המים, The waters dried up, by Gematria are equivalent to נחל כרית, the brook Cherith, where the ravens fed Elias: which, however, is not true.
